title: Contributing to mariposa
text: mariposa’s core claim SPSS-compatible, validated results. Contributions touching statistical code must follow rules: SPSS validation: New statistics need reference values SPSS v29 validation test asserting via assert_spss(). Tolerances come exclusively tier system tests/testthat/helper-validation-tolerances.R — inline numeric tolerances rejected automated discipline test. Weighted formulas live one place: weighted formula belongs R/kernels-weighted.R, never inline function file. Weights invariance: Every weighted entry point must reproduce unweighted result weights == 1. New weighted statistics must add block tests/testthat/test-weights-invariance.R. See .claude/VALIDATION_CHARTER.md repository full policy.

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
text: Correlation measures two variables move together. mariposa provides three methods different situations: three support multiple variables (correlation matrices), grouped analysis, weights argument. Pearson Kendall compute weighted coefficients; Spearman, weights select cases (weight <= 0 missing excludes case) rho unweighted.

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
text: Interpretation r: r = 1: Perfect positive correlation r = 0: linear relationship r = -1: Perfect negative correlation
code: survey_data %>%   pearson_cor(age, income) #> Pearson Correlation: age x income #>   r = -0.007, p = 0.761, N = 2186 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
code: survey_data %>%   pearson_cor(age, income, weights = sampling_weight) #> Pearson Correlation: age x income [Weighted] #>   r = -0.005, p = 0.828, N = 2201 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
text: Pass multiple variables get pairwise correlations:
code: survey_data %>%   pearson_cor(trust_government, trust_media, trust_science,               weights = sampling_weight) #> Pearson Correlation: 3 variables [Weighted] #>   trust_government x trust_media:   r = 0.012, p = 0.582 #>   trust_government x trust_science: r = 0.031, p = 0.145 #>   trust_media x trust_science:      r = 0.024, p = 0.259 #>   0/3 pairs significant (p < .05), N = 2242-2286 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
code: result <- survey_data %>%   pearson_cor(age, income, weights = sampling_weight)  summary(result) #>  #> Weighted Pearson Correlation #> ---------------------------- #>  #> - Weights variable: sampling_weight #> - Missing data handling: pairwise deletion #> - Confidence level: 95.0% #> - Alternative hypothesis: two.sided #>  #>  #>   Correlation: r = -0.005 #>   p-value (2-tailed): p = 0.828 #>   N = 2201 #>   95% CI: [-0.046, 0.037] #>   r-squared: 0.000 #>  #> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
text: Use Spearman’s \rho relationship monotonic necessarily linear, working ordinal data data outliers:
code: survey_data %>%   spearman_rho(political_orientation, environmental_concern,                weights = sampling_weight) #> Spearman Correlation: political_orientation x environmental_concern #>   rho = -0.576, p < 0.001 ***, N = 2207 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
code: survey_data %>%   spearman_rho(political_orientation, environmental_concern,                life_satisfaction, trust_government,                weights = sampling_weight) #> Spearman Correlation: 4 variables #>   political_orientation x environmental_concern: rho = -0.576, p < 0.001 *** #>   political_orientation x life_satisfaction:     rho = -0.004, p = 0.833 #>   political_orientation x trust_government:      rho = -0.055, p = 0.011 * #>   environmental_concern x life_satisfaction:     rho = 0.003, p = 0.904 #>   environmental_concern x trust_government:      rho = 0.067, p = 0.002 ** #>   life_satisfaction x trust_government:          rho = 0.002, p = 0.942 #>   3/6 pairs significant (p < .05), N = 2168-2324 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
text: Use Kendall’s \tau ordinal data, small samples (n < 30), data many tied values. robust Spearman typically produces smaller absolute values:
code: survey_data %>%   kendall_tau(political_orientation, life_satisfaction,               weights = sampling_weight) #> Kendall's Tau: political_orientation x life_satisfaction [Weighted] #>   tau = -0.005, p = 0.747, N = 2241 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
text: partial_cor() (SPSS PARTIAL CORR) removes influence control variables correlation. Comparing partial zero-order correlation shows much original association controls explain: Multiple analysis variables multiple controls work together; three variables, summary() adds partial-correlation matrix:
code: # Does the satisfaction-income correlation survive controlling for age? survey_data %>%   partial_cor(life_satisfaction, income, controls = age,               weights = sampling_weight) #> Partial Correlation: life_satisfaction, income | controlling for age [Weighted] #>   life_satisfaction x income: partial r = 0.450, p < 0.001 *** (zero-order r = 0.450), N = 2130 #> Use summary() for detailed output. result <- survey_data %>%   partial_cor(trust_government, trust_media, trust_science,               controls = c(age, political_orientation)) summary(result) #>  #> Partial Correlation Results #> --------------------------- #> - Variables: trust_government, trust_media, trust_science #> - Controlling for: age, political_orientation #> - Missing: Listwise deletion #>  #> Partial Correlation Matrix: #> --------------------------- #>                   trust_government  trust_media  trust_science #> trust_government                 1        0.019          0.033 #> trust_media                  0.019            1          0.009 #> trust_science                0.033        0.009              1 #> --------------------------- #>  #> Pairwise Results: #>   -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>   Variable 1        Variable 2     Partial r  Zero-order r    df      t     p     n  sig #>   -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>   trust_government  trust_media        0.019         0.019  1960  0.859  .390  1964      #>   trust_government  trust_science      0.033         0.030  1960  1.447  .148  1964      #>   trust_media       trust_science      0.009         0.010  1960  0.407  .684  1964      #>   -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>  #> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
text: Pearson Spearman give different results, relationship may non-linear:
code: pearson_result <- survey_data %>%   pearson_cor(life_satisfaction, income, weights = sampling_weight)  spearman_result <- survey_data %>%   spearman_rho(life_satisfaction, income, weights = sampling_weight)  kendall_result <- survey_data %>%   kendall_tau(life_satisfaction, income, weights = sampling_weight)  comparison <- data.frame(   Method = c("Pearson", "Spearman", "Kendall"),   Correlation = c(pearson_result$correlations$correlation[1],                   spearman_result$correlations$rho[1],                   kendall_result$correlations$tau[1]),   P_Value = c(pearson_result$correlations$p_value[1],               spearman_result$correlations$p_value[1],               kendall_result$correlations$p_value[1]) ) print(comparison) #>     Method Correlation       P_Value #> 1  Pearson   0.4501535 8.997507e-107 #> 2 Spearman   0.4639317 2.322944e-113 #> 3  Kendall   0.3532949 6.963954e-132

title: Understanding Relationships: Correlation Analysis
text: Always check scatterplot. Correlations can miss non-linear relationships, single outlier can inflate deflate coefficient. Use Spearman doubt. makes fewer assumptions Pearson works continuous ordinal data. Report magnitude, just significance. large samples, even r = .05 can significant practically meaningless. Use correlation matrices prioritize. regression, check variables strongly related outcome.

title: Importing and Exporting Data
text: Survey data lives many formats — SPSS (.sav), Stata (.dta), SAS (.sas7bdat), Excel (.xlsx). mariposa reads preserves metadata makes survey data special: variable labels, value labels, missing value definitions. export, mariposa writes data back statistical formats full preservation labels missing values:

title: Importing and Exporting Data
text: SPSS common format survey research. read_spss() reads .sav files preserves metadata: result tibble haven_labelled columns. column carries variable label, value labels, missing value definitions attributes.
code: # Read an SPSS file data <- read_spss("survey_2024.sav")

title: Importing and Exporting Data
text: SPSS allows researchers define multiple types missing values (e.g., -9 = “refused”, -8 = “don’t know”, -7 = “applicable”). default, read_spss() preserves tagged NAs — special NA values remember missing code came :
code: # Tagged NAs are on by default data <- read_spss("survey.sav", tag_na = TRUE)  # Turn off if you just want regular NAs data <- read_spss("survey.sav", tag_na = FALSE)

title: Importing and Exporting Data
text: imported, can inspect tagged NAs: na_frequencies() particularly useful understanding response patterns — shows many respondents refused, said “don’t know”, skipped question.
code: # See a breakdown of missing types na_frequencies(data, q1, q2, q3)  # Convert tagged NAs back to their original codes data_with_codes <- untag_na(data, q1, q2)  # Remove tags but keep NAs data_clean <- strip_tags(data)

title: Importing and Exporting Data
text: key strength mariposa lossless roundtripping. Data imported SPSS can exported back without losing information:
code: # 1. Import from SPSS original <- read_spss("survey.sav")  # 2. Work with the data in R processed <- original %>%   filter(age >= 18) %>%   mutate(age_group = rec(., age, rules = "18:29=1; 30:49=2; 50:99=3"))  # 3. Export back to SPSS write_spss(processed, "survey_processed.sav")  # Variable labels, value labels, and missing value definitions # are all preserved in the exported file.

title: Data Transformation
text: std() z-standardizes variables mean 0 standard deviation 1. useful comparing variables different scales.

title: Data Transformation
Data Transformation
text: std() supports four methods: "sd" (default): Classic z-standardization (\frac{x - \bar{x}}{SD}) "2sd": Gelman’s (2008) recommendation — divides 2 SD, making coefficients comparable untransformed binary predictors "mad": Robust standardization using median MAD (resistant outliers) "gmd": Standardization using Gini Mean Difference
code: # Default: divide by SD survey_data_methods <- survey_data %>%   std(life_satisfaction, method = "sd", suffix = "_sd") %>%   std(life_satisfaction, method = "2sd", suffix = "_2sd") %>%   std(life_satisfaction, method = "mad", suffix = "_mad")  survey_data_methods %>%   describe(life_satisfaction_sd, life_satisfaction_2sd, life_satisfaction_mad,            show = c("mean", "sd")) #>  #> Descriptive Statistics #> ---------------------- #>  #>   --------------------------------------------------- #>   Variable                 Mean     SD     N  Missing #>   --------------------------------------------------- #>   life_satisfaction_sd    0.000  1.000  2421       79 #>   life_satisfaction_2sd   0.000  0.500  2421       79 #>   life_satisfaction_mad  -0.251  0.778  2421       79 #>   ---------------------------------------------------

title: Data Transformation
code: survey_data <- survey_data %>%   std(income, weights = sampling_weight, suffix = "_wstd")  survey_data %>%   describe(income_wstd, show = c("mean", "sd")) #>  #> Descriptive Statistics #> ---------------------- #>  #>   ---------------------------------------- #>   Variable      Mean     SD     N  Missing #>   ---------------------------------------- #>   income_wstd  0.008  1.006  2186      314 #>   ----------------------------------------

title: Data Transformation
text: pomps() transforms scores Percent Maximum Possible Scores scale (0–100). makes scores different scales directly comparable: score 0 means respondent chose minimum every item; 100 means maximum every item. Always specify scale_min scale_max based theoretical scale range, observed range. ensures scores comparable across samples.
code: survey_data <- survey_data %>%   mutate(trust_pomps = pomps(m_trust, scale_min = 1, scale_max = 5))  survey_data %>%   describe(trust_pomps) #>  #> Descriptive Statistics #> ---------------------- #>  #>   ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>   Variable       Mean  Median      SD    Range     IQR  Skewness     N  Missing #>   ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>   trust_pomps  47.885  50.000  17.500  100.000  25.000     0.015  2500        0 #>   ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Transform multiple variables at once survey_data <- survey_data %>%   mutate(across(     c(trust_government, trust_media, trust_science),     ~ pomps(.x, scale_min = 1, scale_max = 5),     .names = "{.col}_pomps"   ))

title: Data Transformation
text: typical data transformation workflow analysis:
code: data(survey_data)  # fresh copy  # 1. Recode: create age groups and reverse-code an item survey_data <- rec(survey_data, age,   rules = "18:29=1 [Young]; 30:49=2 [Middle]; 50:99=3 [Older]",   suffix = "_group", as_factor = TRUE) survey_data <- rec(survey_data, trust_government,   rules = "rev(1, 5)", suffix = "_rev")  # 2. Create scale score survey_data <- survey_data %>%   mutate(m_trust = row_means(., trust_government, trust_media, trust_science,                              min_valid = 2))  # 3. Standardize for regression survey_data <- survey_data %>%   std(age, income, suffix = "_z")  # 4. Use in analysis survey_data %>%   t_test(m_trust, group = gender, weights = sampling_weight) #> t-Test: m_trust by gender [Weighted] #>   t(2457.6) = -2.362, p = 0.018 *, g = -0.095 (negligible), N = 2499 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  survey_data %>%   linear_regression(life_satisfaction ~ age_z + income_z + m_trust,                     weights = sampling_weight) #> Linear Regression: life_satisfaction ~ age_z + income_z + m_trust [Weighted] #>   R2 = 0.201, adj.R2 = 0.200, F(3, 2109) = 177.02, p < 0.001 ***, N = 2113 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Data Transformation
text: Use rec() survey-specific recoding. string syntax readable nested ifelse() case_when() typical survey transformations. Always specify min_valid row_means(). Without , respondent answered 1 10 items gets scale score based single response. Setting min_valid half number items common rule thumb. Center variables regression. Centering makes intercept interpretable expected value mean predictors. Group-mean centering separates within-group -group effects. Use std(method = "2sd") mixed models. Gelman (2008) recommends dividing 2 SD standardized coefficients continuous predictors comparable binary predictors. Always use theoretical min/max pomps(). Using observed min/max makes scores sample-dependent non-comparable.

title: Comparing Groups and Testing Hypotheses
text: parametric tests first row assume (approximately) normally distributed variables. normality_test() produces SPSS EXAMINE “Tests Normality” table — Kolmogorov-Smirnov Lilliefors correction Shapiro-Wilk: Run grouped () compare groups: assumption matters normality within group. large samples tests flag even trivial deviations, combine skewness kurtosis describe() switching non-parametric alternative.
code: survey_data %>%   group_by(gender) %>%   normality_test(age, income) #> Normality Tests: age, income [Grouped: gender] #> [gender = Male] #>   age: KS = 0.029, p = 0.018; Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.989, p < 0.001 (n = 1194) #>   income: KS = 0.080, p < 0.001; Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.960, p < 0.001 (n = 1046) #> [gender = Female] #>   age: KS = 0.030, p = 0.007; Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.990, p < 0.001 (n = 1306) #>   income: KS = 0.081, p < 0.001; Shapiro-Wilk W = 0.965, p < 0.001 (n = 1140) #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Comparing Groups and Testing Hypotheses
text: Compare two groups continuous variable: output includes Student’s t-test (equal variances assumed) Welch’s t-test (assumed). doubt, use Welch — robust. detailed output group descriptives, Levene’s test, confidence intervals:
code: survey_data %>%   t_test(life_satisfaction, group = gender, weights = sampling_weight) #> t-Test: life_satisfaction by gender [Weighted] #>   t(2391.3) = -1.069, p = 0.285, g = -0.043 (negligible), N = 2436 #> Use summary() for detailed output. survey_data %>%   t_test(life_satisfaction, group = gender, weights = sampling_weight) %>%   summary() #> Weighted t-Test Results #> ----------------------- #>  #> - Grouping variable: gender #> - Groups compared: Male vs. Female #> - Weights variable: sampling_weight #> - Confidence level: 95.0% #> - Alternative hypothesis: two.sided #> - Null hypothesis (mu): 0.000 #>  #> --- life_satisfaction --- #>  #> Weighted Group Statistics: #>   ---------------------------------------------------- #>   gender     N   Mean  Std. Deviation  Std. Error Mean #>   ---------------------------------------------------- #>   Male    1149  3.598           1.165            0.034 #>   Female  1287  3.648           1.141            0.032 #>   ---------------------------------------------------- #>  #> Weighted Independent Samples Test: #>   -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>                                     t        df     p  Mean Diff.  SE Diff.  95% CI Lower  95% CI Upper    #>   -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>   Equal variances assumed      -1.070      2435  .285      -0.050     0.047        -0.142         0.042    #>   Equal variances not assumed  -1.069  2391.291  .285      -0.050     0.047        -0.142         0.042    #>   -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>  #> Effect Sizes: #>   ----------------------------------------------------------------- #>   Variable           Cohen's d  Hedges' g  Glass' Delta   Magnitude #>   ----------------------------------------------------------------- #>   life_satisfaction     -0.043     -0.043        -0.043  negligible #>   ----------------------------------------------------------------- #>  #> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 #>  #> Effect Size Interpretation: #> - Cohen's d: pooled standard deviation (classic) #> - Hedges' g: bias-corrected Cohen's d (preferred) #> - Glass' Delta: control group standard deviation only #> - Small effect: |effect| ~ 0.2 #> - Medium effect: |effect| ~ 0.5 #> - Large effect: |effect| ~ 0.8

title: Comparing Groups and Testing Hypotheses
text: Compare means across three groups: effect size \eta^2 (eta-squared) indicates much variance explained group membership: Small: \eta^2 \approx 0.01 Medium: \eta^2 \approx 0.06 Large: \eta^2 \approx 0.14
code: result <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education, weights = sampling_weight) result #> One-Way ANOVA: life_satisfaction by education [Weighted] #>   F(3, 2432) = 65.333, p < 0.001 ***, eta2 = 0.075 (medium), N = 2437 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Comparing Groups and Testing Hypotheses
text: significant ANOVA tells groups differ, groups. Use post-hoc tests:
code: # Tukey HSD: balanced comparison of all pairs tukey_test(result) #> Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test by education [Weighted] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table. # Scheffe: more conservative (fewer false positives) scheffe_test(result) #> Scheffe Post-Hoc Test by education [Weighted] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 4 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.

title: Comparing Groups and Testing Hypotheses
text: ANOVA assumes equal variances. Test Levene’s test: Levene’s test significant (p < .05), variances unequal. Use Welch correction included ANOVA output.
code: levene_test(result) #> Levene's Test: life_satisfaction by education [Weighted] #>   F(3, 2432.6) = 31.282, p < 0.001 ***, variances unequal #> Use summary() for detailed output.

Dependent variable: life_satisfaction #> - Factors: gender x region #> - Sum of squares: Type III #> - Weights variable: sampling_weight #> - N (complete cases): 2421 #> - Missing: 79 #>  #> Tests of Between-Subjects Effects #>   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>   Source           Type III Sum of Squares    df  Mean Square          F    Sig  Partial Eta Squared      #>   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>   Corrected Model                    3.714     3        1.238      0.927   .427                0.001      #>   Intercept                      20468.612     1    20468.612  15319.285  <.001                0.864  *** #>   gender                             0.010     1        0.010      0.008   .930                0.000      #>   region                             0.001     1        0.001      0.001   .979                0.000      #>   gender * region                    2.194     1        2.194      1.642   .200                0.001      #>   Error                           3229.435  2417        1.336                                             #>   Total                          35249.294  2421                                                          #>   Corrected Total                 3233.149  2420                                                          #>   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #> R Squared = 0.001 (Adjusted R Squared = 0.000) #>  #> Descriptive Statistics #>   ------------------------------------------- #>   gender  region   Mean  Std. title: Comparing Groups and Testing Hypotheses
text: non-parametric alternative one-way ANOVA (3+ groups): significant, use Dunn’s post-hoc test Bonferroni correction:
code: kw_result <- survey_data %>%   kruskal_wallis(life_satisfaction, group = education)  kw_result #> Kruskal-Wallis Test: life_satisfaction by education #>   H(3) = 171.178, p < 0.001 ***, eps2 = 0.071 (medium), N = 2421 #> Use summary() for detailed output. dunn_test(kw_result) #> Dunn Post-Hoc Test (Bonferroni) by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.

text: non-parametric alternative paired t-test:
code: data(longitudinal_data_wide)  longitudinal_data_wide %>%   wilcoxon_test(score_T1, score_T2) #> Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test: score_T2 - score_T1 #>   Z = -5.427, p < 0.001 ***, r = 0.530 (large), N = 105 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Comparing Groups and Testing Hypotheses
text: non-parametric alternative repeated-measures ANOVA (3+ measurements): significant, use pairwise Wilcoxon post-hoc tests:
code: friedman_result <- longitudinal_data_wide %>%   friedman_test(score_T1, score_T2, score_T3)  friedman_result #> Friedman Test: score_T1, score_T2, score_T3 #>   chi2(2) = 47.255, p < 0.001 ***, Kendall's W = 0.251 (weak), N = 94 #> Use summary() for detailed output. pairwise_wilcoxon(friedman_result) #> Pairwise Wilcoxon Post-Hoc Test (Bonferroni) #>   3 comparisons, 3 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Survey data SPSS, Stata, SAS stores two kinds labels: Variable labels describe variable measures (e.g., gender → “Respondent’s gender”) Value labels map numeric codes text (e.g., 1 → “Male”, 2 → “Female”) R, labels stored attributes haven_labelled columns. mariposa provides 10 functions inspecting, modifying, converting labelled data — plus tools declaring missing values searching variables.

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Variable labels describe column contains. Use var_label() retrieve :
code: # Get labels for specific variables var_label(survey_data, gender, education, life_satisfaction) #>                                            gender  #>                                          "Gender"  #>                                         education  #>                  "Highest educational attainment"  #>                                 life_satisfaction  #> "Life satisfaction (1=dissatisfied, 5=satisfied)" # Get labels for all variables var_label(survey_data) #>                                                id  #>                                                NA  #>                                               age  #>                                    "Age in years"  #>                                            gender  #>                                          "Gender"  #>                                            region  #>                              "Region (East/West)"  #>                                         education  #>                  "Highest educational attainment"  #>                                            income  #>                  "Monthly household income (EUR)"  #>                                        employment  #>                               "Employment status"  #>                             political_orientation  #>         "Political orientation (1=left, 5=right)"  #>                             environmental_concern  #>           "Environmental concern (1=low, 5=high)"  #>                                 life_satisfaction  #> "Life satisfaction (1=dissatisfied, 5=satisfied)"  #>                                  trust_government  #>        "Trust in government (1=none, 5=complete)"  #>                                       trust_media  #>             "Trust in media (1=none, 5=complete)"  #>                                     trust_science  #>           "Trust in science (1=none, 5=complete)"  #>                                   sampling_weight  #>                                "Weighting factor"  #>                                           stratum  #>                         "Stratification variable"  #>                                    interview_mode  #>                                  "Interview mode"

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Value labels map numeric codes meaningful text. Use val_labels() retrieve :
code: # Get value labels for a single variable val_labels(survey_data, gender) #> NULL # Get value labels for multiple variables val_labels(survey_data, education, employment) #> $education #> NULL #>  #> $employment #> NULL

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: SPSS datasets often cryptic variable names like q104a_1 v23. Use find_var() search name label:
code: # Search in both names and labels (default) find_var(survey_data, "trust") #>   col             name                                    label #> 1  11 trust_government Trust in government (1=none, 5=complete) #> 2  12      trust_media      Trust in media (1=none, 5=complete) #> 3  13    trust_science    Trust in science (1=none, 5=complete) # Search only in variable labels find_var(survey_data, "satisfaction", search = "label") #>   col              name                                           label #> 1  10 life_satisfaction Life satisfaction (1=dissatisfied, 5=satisfied) # Search only in variable names find_var(survey_data, "age|income", search = "name") #>   col   name                          label #> 1   2    age                   Age in years #> 2   6 income Monthly household income (EUR)

title: Labels and Missing Values
code: # Set labels for specific variables labeled_data <- var_label(survey_data,   age = "Age of respondent in years",   income = "Monthly net income in euros" )  # Verify var_label(labeled_data, age, income) #>                           age                        income  #>  "Age of respondent in years" "Monthly net income in euros"

title: Labels and Missing Values
code: # Set value labels on a numeric (1-5) rating labeled_data <- val_labels(survey_data,   life_satisfaction = c("Very dissatisfied" = 1, "Very satisfied" = 5) )  # Verify val_labels(labeled_data, life_satisfaction) #> Very dissatisfied    Very satisfied  #>                 1                 5 # Add labels without replacing existing ones labeled_data <- val_labels(labeled_data,   life_satisfaction = c("Neither" = 3),   .add = TRUE )  val_labels(labeled_data, life_satisfaction) #> Very dissatisfied    Very satisfied           Neither  #>                 1                 5                 3

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Survey data often needs conversion labelled, factor, character, numeric formats depending analysis.

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Use to_label() need factors plotting statistical models:
code: # Labelled variables become factors (factors such as gender pass through) factor_data <- to_label(survey_data, gender, education)  # Check the result class(factor_data$gender) #> [1] "factor" levels(factor_data$gender) #> [1] "Male"   "Female" head(factor_data$gender) #> [1] Female Male   Male   Female Male   Female #> Levels: Male Female # Create ordered factors (useful for ordinal variables) ordered_data <- to_label(survey_data, education, ordered = TRUE) levels(ordered_data$education) #> [1] "Basic Secondary"        "Intermediate Secondary" "Academic Secondary"     #> [4] "University"

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Use to_character() string-based operations:
code: char_data <- to_character(survey_data, gender, region) head(char_data$gender) #> [1] "Female" "Male"   "Male"   "Female" "Male"   "Female"

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Use to_numeric() convert factors labelled vectors back numbers:
code: # First convert to factor, then back to numeric factor_data <- to_label(survey_data, education)  # Parse numeric values from factor levels numeric_data <- to_numeric(factor_data, education) head(numeric_data$education) #> [1] 2 3 3 1 1 2

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Use to_labelled() add labels plain numeric factor columns:
code: # Convert a factor back to haven_labelled plain_data <- data.frame(   gender = factor(c("Male", "Female", "Male")),   score = c(3, 4, 2) )  labelled_data <- to_labelled(plain_data, gender) class(labelled_data$gender) #> [1] "haven_labelled" "vctrs_vctr"     "double"

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Use set_na() declare specific numeric codes missing values: tag = TRUE (default), missing code becomes distinct tagged NA, can later distinguish “refused” “don’t know” responses.
code: # After importing SPSS data where -9 = refused, -8 = don't know data <- read_spss("survey.sav", tag_na = FALSE)  # Declare -9 and -8 as missing across all numeric columns data <- set_na(data, -9, -8, tag = TRUE)  # Declare different missing codes for specific variables data <- set_na(data, q1 = c(-9, -8), q2 = c(99))

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Use unlabel() need plain numeric data without label metadata: converts haven_labelled columns plain numeric character, tagged NAs regular NA, removes label attributes.
code: # Strip all labels from entire dataset plain_data <- unlabel(survey_data)  # Strip labels from specific variables only plain_data <- unlabel(survey_data, gender, education)

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: dplyr operations like filter(), mutate(), select() can strip label attributes columns:
code: filtered <- survey_data %>%   filter(age >= 30) %>%   select(gender, education, income)  # Labels may be lost after certain operations

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Use copy_labels() restore labels original data:
code: # Restore labels from the source dataset filtered <- copy_labels(filtered, survey_data)  # Verify labels are back var_label(filtered, gender, education) #>                           gender                        education  #>                         "Gender" "Highest educational attainment"

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: filtering, value label categories may longer appear data. Use drop_labels() clean :
code: # Subset to one region only subset_data <- survey_data %>% filter(region == 1)  # Remove value labels for regions that are no longer in the data clean_data <- drop_labels(subset_data, region) val_labels(clean_data, region) #> NULL

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: typical workflow preparing SPSS data analysis:
code: # 1. Import SPSS file data <- read_spss("survey_2024.sav")  # 2. Explore what's in the data codebook(data) find_var(data, "satisf") find_var(data, "trust")  # 3. Check labels var_label(data, q1, q2, q3) val_labels(data, q1)  # 4. Rename variables for clarity data <- data %>%   rename(life_satisfaction = q1, income = q2, education = q3)  # Update variable labels data <- var_label(data,   life_satisfaction = "Overall life satisfaction (1-5)",   income = "Monthly net income in euros",   education = "Highest education level" )  # 5. Convert categorical variables for analysis data <- to_label(data, education, gender)  # 6. Analyze data %>%   describe(life_satisfaction, income, weights = sampling_weight)  data %>%   t_test(life_satisfaction, group = gender, weights = sampling_weight)

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: Keep labels long possible. Labels carry important context. convert factor character specific function requires . Use find_var() instead names(). searches names labels, essential SPSS datasets non-descriptive variable names. Use copy_labels() complex pipelines. pipeline involves joins, reshaping, operations might strip attributes, restore labels original data. Prefer to_label() .factor(). to_label() uses value labels factor levels, giving meaningful names instead numeric codes. Use set_na() early workflow. Declaring missing values immediately import ensures handled correctly downstream analyses.

title: Labels and Missing Values
text: var_label() val_labels() get set variable value labels find_var() searches variables name label pattern to_label(), to_character(), to_numeric(), to_labelled() convert formats set_na() declares values missing; unlabel() strips metadata copy_labels() restores labels dplyr operations; drop_labels() cleans unused labels

title: Regression Analysis
text: Regression analysis predicts outcome one predictors. mariposa provides two regression functions SPSS-compatible output: functions support two interface styles: Formula: linear_regression(data, y ~ x1 + x2) — standard R syntax SPSS-style: linear_regression(data, dependent = y, predictors = c(x1, x2))

title: Regression Analysis
code: linear_regression(survey_data, life_satisfaction ~ age) #> Linear Regression: life_satisfaction ~ age #>   R2 = 0.001, adj.R2 = 0.000, F(1, 2419) = 2.00, p = 0.158, N = 2421 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
text: detailed output includes four sections matching SPSS REGRESSION: Model Summary: R, R-squared, Adjusted R-squared ANOVA Table: Overall model significance Coefficients: B (unstandardized), Beta (standardized), t, p, confidence intervals Descriptives: Mean SD variables

title: Regression Analysis
text: B (unstandardized): 1-unit increase predictor, outcome changes B units Beta (standardized): Allows comparison across predictors different scales. Beta 0.30 means 1-SD increase predictor associated 0.30-SD change outcome p-value: 0.05 indicates statistical significance

title: Regression Analysis
text: Compare Beta values identify strongest predictor.
code: linear_regression(survey_data,                   life_satisfaction ~ age + income + trust_government) #> Linear Regression: life_satisfaction ~ age + income + trust_government #>   R2 = 0.198, adj.R2 = 0.197, F(3, 1991) = 163.89, p < 0.001 ***, N = 1995 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
code: linear_regression(survey_data,                   dependent = life_satisfaction,                   predictors = c(age, income, trust_government)) #> Linear Regression: life_satisfaction ~ age + income + trust_government #>   R2 = 0.198, adj.R2 = 0.197, F(3, 1991) = 163.89, p < 0.001 ***, N = 1995 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
text: Weights treated frequency weights, matching SPSS WEIGHT behavior.
code: linear_regression(survey_data,                   life_satisfaction ~ age + income,                   weights = sampling_weight) #> Linear Regression: life_satisfaction ~ age + income [Weighted] #>   R2 = 0.203, adj.R2 = 0.202, F(2, 2127) = 270.42, p < 0.001 ***, N = 2130 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
text: Run separate regressions subgroup:
code: survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   linear_regression(life_satisfaction ~ age + income) #> Linear Regression: life_satisfaction ~ age + income [Grouped: region] #> [region = East] #>   R2 = 0.203, adj.R2 = 0.199, F(2, 407) = 51.95, p < 0.001 ***, N = 410 #> [region = West] #>   R2 = 0.201, adj.R2 = 0.200, F(2, 1702) = 214.58, p < 0.001 ***, N = 1705 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
text: R-squared tells much variance predictors explain: 0.01 – 0.05: Small effect 0.06 – 0.13: Medium effect 0.14+: Large effect benchmarks follow Cohen (1988). Always check ANOVA table confirm overall model significance.

title: Regression Analysis
text: Combine data transformation functions better models:
code: # Standardize predictors for comparable coefficients survey_data_z <- survey_data %>%   std(age, income, suffix = "_z")  linear_regression(survey_data_z,                   life_satisfaction ~ age_z + income_z + trust_government,                   weights = sampling_weight) #> Linear Regression: life_satisfaction ~ age_z + income_z + trust_government [Weighted] #>   R2 = 0.200, adj.R2 = 0.199, F(3, 2005) = 167.49, p < 0.001 ***, N = 2009 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
text: Use logistic_regression() outcome binary. First, create binary variable:
code: survey_data <- survey_data %>%   mutate(high_satisfaction = ifelse(life_satisfaction >= 4, 1, 0))

title: Regression Analysis
code: logistic_regression(survey_data, high_satisfaction ~ age + income) #> Logistic Regression: high_satisfaction ~ age + income [P(high_satisfaction = 1)] #>   Nagelkerke R2 = 0.209, chi2(2) = 357.43, p < 0.001 ***, Accuracy = 68.4%, N = 2115 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
text: detailed output includes five sections matching SPSS LOGISTIC REGRESSION: Omnibus Test: Overall model significance Model Summary: -2 Log Likelihood pseudo R-squared values Hosmer-Lemeshow Test: Model fit assessment Classification Table: Prediction accuracy Coefficients: B, Wald, Exp(B) (odds ratios), confidence intervals

title: Regression Analysis
text: Exp(B) odds ratio — key statistic logistic regression: Exp(B) > 1: unit increase raises odds (e.g., 1.50 = 50% higher odds) Exp(B) < 1: unit increase lowers odds (e.g., 0.80 = 20% lower odds) Exp(B) = 1: effect

title: Regression Analysis
code: logistic_regression(survey_data,                     high_satisfaction ~ age + income + trust_government + education) #> Logistic Regression: high_satisfaction ~ age + income + trust_government + education [P(high_satisfaction = 1)] #>   Nagelkerke R2 = 0.212, chi2(6) = 341.28, p < 0.001 ***, Accuracy = 68.1%, N = 1995 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
code: logistic_regression(survey_data,                     dependent = high_satisfaction,                     predictors = c(age, income, trust_government)) #> Logistic Regression: high_satisfaction ~ age + income + trust_government [P(high_satisfaction = 1)] #>   Nagelkerke R2 = 0.207, chi2(3) = 333.76, p < 0.001 ***, Accuracy = 68.4%, N = 1995 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
code: logistic_regression(survey_data,                     high_satisfaction ~ age + income,                     weights = sampling_weight) #> Logistic Regression: high_satisfaction ~ age + income [P(high_satisfaction = 1)] [Weighted] #>   Nagelkerke R2 = 0.211, chi2(2) = 362.91, p < 0.001 ***, Accuracy = 68.3%, N = 2130 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
code: survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   logistic_regression(high_satisfaction ~ age + income) #> Logistic Regression: high_satisfaction ~ age + income [P(high_satisfaction = 1)] [Grouped: region] #> [region = East] #>   Nagelkerke R2 = 0.178, chi2(2) = 57.88, p < 0.001 ***, Accuracy = 66.8%, N = 410 #> [region = West] #>   Nagelkerke R2 = 0.218, chi2(2) = 301.11, p < 0.001 ***, Accuracy = 68.8%, N = 1705 #> Use summary() for detailed output.

title: Regression Analysis
text: Pseudo R-squared values directly comparable linear regression R-squared: Nagelkerke R-squared: Adjusted reach 1.0, commonly reported Cox & Snell R-squared: reach 1.0, always lower McFadden R-squared: Values 0.20 indicate good fit Hosmer-Lemeshow Test: Non-significant (p > .05) means model fits well. Classification Table: Compare correct predictions base rate — model outperform guessing common category.

title: Regression Analysis
text: Odds ratios hard communicate. marginal_effects() (Stata’s margins, dydx(*)) translates model onto probability scale: average change predicted probability per unit predictor, delta-method standard errors. Factor predictors show average discrete change reference level: AME 0.03 reads: “one unit increases probability outcome 3 percentage points, averaged sample” — usually sentence readers actually need.
code: model <- survey_data %>%   logistic_regression(high_satisfaction ~ age + income + education)  marginal_effects(model) #> Average Marginal Effects: high_satisfaction ~ age + income + education #>   age: AME = 1.99e-04, p = 0.730 #>   income: AME = 1.43e-04, p < 0.001 *** #>   education: Intermediate Secondary vs. Basic Secondary: AME = 0.059, p = 0.023 * #>   education: Academic Secondary vs. Basic Secondary: AME = 0.015, p = 0.600 #>   education: University vs. Basic Secondary: AME = -0.014, p = 0.715 #> AME = average change in predicted probability. Use summary() for detailed output. summary(marginal_effects(model)) #>  #> Average Marginal Effects Results #> -------------------------------- #> - Formula: high_satisfaction ~ age + income + education #> - Scale: Predicted probability #> - Std. errors: Delta method #> - N: 2115 #>  #>   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>   Term                                                        AME        SE       z      p  95% CI Lower  95% CI Upper      #>   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>   age                                                    1.99e-04     0.001   0.344   .730        -0.001         0.001      #>   income                                                 1.43e-04  8.48e-06  16.833  <.001      1.26e-04      1.59e-04  *** #>   education: Intermediate Secondary vs. Basic Secondary     0.059     0.026   2.268   .023         0.008         0.110    * #>   education: Academic Secondary vs. Basic Secondary         0.015     0.029   0.525   .600        -0.041         0.071      #>   education: University vs. Basic Secondary                -0.014     0.038  -0.365   .715        -0.088         0.061      #>   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #>  #> Factor rows show the average discrete change vs. the reference level. #>  #> Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05

title: Regression Analysis
text: Check correlations first. Use pearson_cor() explore bivariate relationships building model. Center standardize predictors. Centering makes intercept interpretable; standardizing (std()) makes Beta coefficients comparable. Use std(method = "2sd") make continuous predictors comparable binary ones. Compare Beta values. multiple regression, standardized Beta coefficients reveal predictor strongest effect, regardless measurement scale. Watch multicollinearity. Highly correlated predictors produce unstable coefficients. Check bivariate correlations interpreting results. Never use linear_regression() binary outcome. Predicted values can fall outside 0–1, statistical tests invalid. Use logistic_regression() instead. Report completely. Include R-squared, F-test Omnibus test, individual coefficients, sample size.

title: Regression Analysis
text: linear_regression() predicts continuous outcomes (B, Beta, ANOVA, R-squared) logistic_regression() predicts binary outcomes (odds ratios, classification, pseudo R-squared) support formula SPSS-style interfaces, survey weights, grouped analysis Use std() center() prepare predictors better interpretability Always explore bivariate relationships building regression models

title: Scale Analysis
text: Always check reliability first. mean index unreliable items produces meaningless results. Aim Alpha > .70. Use min_valid wisely. 3–5 item scales, min_valid = 2 reasonable compromise. longer scales, require least half items. Specify theoretical scale_min / scale_max pomps(). Using observed values makes scores sample-dependent non-comparable. Run EFA 6+ items. Factor analysis can reveal unexpected dimensions create indices. Check grouped reliability. scale works well overall may unreliable specific subgroups (e.g., different regions education levels).

code: # Without weights (describes the sample) unweighted <- survey_data %>%   summarise(     mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),     mean_income = mean(income, na.rm = TRUE)   )  # With weights (represents the population) age_w <- w_mean(survey_data, age, weights = sampling_weight) income_w <- w_mean(survey_data, income, weights = sampling_weight)  comparison <- data.frame(   Variable = c("Age", "Income"),   Unweighted = c(unweighted$mean_age, unweighted$mean_income),   Weighted = c(age_w$results$weighted_mean, income_w$results$weighted_mean) ) print(comparison) #>   Variable Unweighted  Weighted #> 1      Age    50.5496   50.5144 #> 2   Income  3753.9341 3743.0994

title: Working with Survey Weights
text: Weighting reduces statistical precision. effective sample size (n_{eff}) tells much information weighted sample actually carries: n_{eff} = \frac{\left(\sum w_i\right)^2}{\sum w_i^2} design effect 1.0 means weights impact precision. Values 1 mean larger standard errors unweighted sample size.
code:
actual_n <- nrow(survey_data) age_w <- w_mean(survey_data, age, weights = sampling_weight) effective_n <- age_w$results$effective_n  cat("Actual sample size:", actual_n, "
") #> Actual sample size: 2500 cat("Effective sample size:", round(effective_n), "
") #> Effective sample size: 2469 cat("Design effect:", round(actual_n / effective_n, 2), "
") #> Design effect: 1.01

title: Working with Survey Weights
text: Always use weights provided. correct sampling biases make results generalizable. Report weighted unweighted sample sizes. actual n tells readers data collection; effective n tells statistical precision. Check extreme weights. Large variation inflates standard errors reduces statistical power. Consider trimming necessary. Document weight source. Explain weights calculated adjust (e.g., age, gender, region post-stratification). Report effective sample size. tells readers much precision lost due weighting.

title: Analysis of Covariance: ANCOVA — ancova
text: ancova() tests whether group means differ controlling one continuous covariates. performs factorial ANCOVA using Type III Sum Squares, matching SPSS UNIANOVA output keyword. Think : ANOVA removes effect confounding variables first Testing group differences "adjusted" means Combining regression (covariates) ANOVA (factors) one model test tells : Whether factor significant effect controlling covariates relationship covariate outcome Effect sizes factors covariates (partial eta squared) Estimated marginal means (group means adjusted covariates)

title: Analysis of Covariance: ANCOVA — ancova
code: ancova(data, dv, between, covariate, weights = NULL, ss_type = 3)

title: Analysis of Covariance: ANCOVA — ancova
text: data survey data (data frame tibble) dv numeric dependent variable analyze (unquoted) Character vector unquoted variable names specifying -subjects factors (1-3 factors). must categorical variables (factor, character, labelled numeric). covariate Unquoted variable names continuous covariates control . Use c(age, income) multiple covariates. weights Optional survey weights population-representative results. Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. ss_type Deprecated; 3 (Type III, SPSS default) implemented. Passing 2 issues warning computes Type III.

title: Analysis of Covariance: ANCOVA — ancova
text: object class "ancova" containing: anova_table Tibble Source, SS, df, MS, F, p, Partial Eta Squared parameter_estimates Tibble regression coefficients (B, SE, t, p, CI, partial eta squared) SPSS coding: one row per category, last category factor reference reported redundant 0 (redundant = TRUE) descriptives Tibble unadjusted cell means, SDs, Ns estimated_marginal_means Tibble adjusted cell means (covariates grand mean) emm_main_effects 2+ factors: named list tibbles adjusted main-effect means (unweighted average cell means, SPSS /EMMEANS=TABLES(factor)); NULL one factor levene_test Tibble Levene's test equality error variances (f, df1, df2, p): SPSS UNIANOVA, one-way ANOVA absolute residuals ANCOVA model across cells design. Also available levene_test(result). r_squared R-squared Adjusted R-squared model underlying lm model object call_info List metadata (dv, factors, covariates, weighted, etc.) Use summary() full SPSS-style output toggleable sections. data grouped group_by(), one ANCOVA computed per group: tables carry group keys leading columns group_results holds complete result group (NULL, warning, group analysed).

title: Analysis of Covariance: ANCOVA — ancova
text: Adjusted Means (Estimated Marginal Means): group means statistically removing effect covariate(s). answer: "group means groups covariate values?" Covariate Effects: covariate row ANOVA table shows whether covariate significantly predicts DV adjusting factors. Factor Effects: show whether factor affects DV controlling covariate. primary test interest. Partial Eta Squared (Effect Size): Less 0.01: Negligible 0.01 0.06: Small 0.06 0.14: Medium 0.14 greater: Large

title: Analysis of Covariance: ANCOVA — ancova
text: Use ANCOVA : group comparisons (ANOVA) want control confound covariate continuous linearly related DV want increase statistical power removing known variance sources covariate's relationship DV across groups (homogeneity regression slopes assumption)

title: Test If Two Categories Are Related — chi_square

Reported every table, SPSS ; 2x2 table equals Cramer's V, larger tables can exceed 1 (use Cramer's V ) Gamma: two ordinal variables (-1 +1, shows direction relationship). Shown summary() variables ordered factors numeric; nominal variables sign depends arbitrary category order. goodman_gamma() always computes .

title: Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test — chisq_gof
text: chisq_gof() tests whether observed frequencies categorical variable match expected frequencies. default, tests equal proportions (uniform distribution). can also specify custom expected proportions. title: Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test — chisq_gof
text: data survey data (data frame tibble) ... One categorical variables test (tidyselect supported) expected Optional numeric vector expected proportions, one per category. NULL (default), equal proportions assumed (SPSS /EXPECTED=EQUAL). Applied every selected variable, variable must many categories. named vector matched categories name (category label, code labelled variable); unnamed vector used category order. title: Remove Unused Value Labels — drop_labels
text: useful subsetting data (e.g., filtering category). removed category's label still exists variable, can cause confusing output frequency() codebook(). drop_labels() cleans keeping labels values actually present data. factors, unused levels dropped; variable label original codes to_label() factor kept. default, tagged NA labels preserved (drop_na = FALSE) represent missing value types, substantive categories.

title: Remove Unused Value Labels — drop_labels
code: # After filtering, "Basic Secondary" no longer occurs but remains a level data_subset <- dplyr::filter(survey_data, education != "Basic Secondary") levels(data_subset$education) #> [1] "Basic Secondary"        "Intermediate Secondary" "Academic Secondary"     #> [4] "University"             data_clean <- drop_labels(data_subset) levels(data_clean$education) #> [1] "Intermediate Secondary" "Academic Secondary"     "University"              # Value labels of labelled vectors if (requireNamespace("haven", quietly = TRUE)) {   x <- haven::labelled(c(1, 2, 2), labels = c(low = 1, mid = 2, high = 3))   drop_labels(x)   # the unused label "high" is removed } #> <labelled<double>[3]> #> [1] 1 2 2 #>  #> Labels: #>  value label #>      1   low #>      2   mid

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After Kruskal-Wallis — dunn_test

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After Kruskal-Wallis — dunn_test
text: Z-Statistics: Based differences mean ranks groups Large absolute Z values indicate big rank differences Positive Z: First group higher mean rank second Negative Z: Second group higher mean rank first Adjusted P-values: Control multiple comparisons p < 0.05: Groups significantly different p >= 0.05: significant difference groups

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After Kruskal-Wallis — dunn_test

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After Kruskal-Wallis — dunn_test
code: # Load required packages and data library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Perform Kruskal-Wallis followed by Dunn post-hoc test kw_result <- survey_data %>%   kruskal_wallis(life_satisfaction, group = education)  # Dunn post-hoc comparisons (default: Bonferroni) kw_result %>% dunn_test() #> Dunn Post-Hoc Test (Bonferroni) by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # With Holm correction (less conservative) kw_result %>% dunn_test(p_adjust = "holm") #> Dunn Post-Hoc Test (Holm) by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 6 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # With Benjamini-Hochberg (controls false discovery rate) kw_result %>% dunn_test(p_adjust = "BH") #> Dunn Post-Hoc Test (Benjamini-Hochberg) by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 6 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # With weights kw_weighted <- survey_data %>%   kruskal_wallis(life_satisfaction, group = education,                  weights = sampling_weight)  kw_weighted %>% dunn_test() #> Dunn Post-Hoc Test (Bonferroni) by education [Weighted] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Multiple variables kw_multi <- survey_data %>%   kruskal_wallis(life_satisfaction, trust_government,                  group = education)  kw_multi %>% dunn_test() #> Dunn Post-Hoc Test (Bonferroni) by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #>   trust_government: 6 comparisons, 0 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Grouped analysis kw_grouped <- survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   kruskal_wallis(life_satisfaction, group = education)  kw_grouped %>% dunn_test() #> Dunn Post-Hoc Test (Bonferroni) by education #> [region = East] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 2 significant (p < .05) #> [region = West] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.

what: Explore the Structure Behind Your Survey Items — efa
title: Explore the Structure Behind Your Survey Items — efa
text: efa() performs Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) discover underlying patterns survey items. Supports Principal Component Analysis (PCA) Maximum Likelihood (ML) extraction. R equivalent SPSS's FACTOR procedure. example, 6 items measuring different attitudes, EFA can reveal whether group 2-3 underlying dimensions (factors components).

title: Explore the Structure Behind Your Survey Items — efa
code: efa(   data,   ...,   n_factors = NULL,   rotation = "varimax",   extraction = "pca",   weights = NULL,   use = "pairwise",   sort = TRUE,   blank = 0.4,   na.rm = TRUE )

title: Explore the Structure Behind Your Survey Items — efa
text: data survey data (data frame tibble) ... items analyze. Use bare column names separated commas, tidyselect helpers like starts_with("trust"). n_factors Number components extract (whole number). Default NULL uses Kaiser criterion (eigenvalue > 1). single component rotated; shown unrotated SPSS's note. rotation Rotation method: "varimax" (default, orthogonal), "oblimin" (oblique direct oblimin, delta = 0, allows correlated factors), "promax" (oblique, power 4), "none". rotations use Kaiser normalization SPSS FACTOR's algorithms stopping rules (25 iterations, SPSS /CRITERIA   ITERATE(25)), reproduce SPSS's rotated matrices; differ slightly stats::varimax(), stats::promax() GPArotation::oblimin(). extraction Extraction method: "pca" (default, Principal Component Analysis) "ml" (Maximum Likelihood, enables goodness--fit testing, assumes multivariate normality). ML uses SPSS's starting values, bounds Heywood variable's communality .999 SPSS keeps SPSS's factor order. weights Optional survey weights population-representative results. Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. use handle missing data correlation computation: "pairwise" (default, matches SPSS) "complete" (listwise; "listwise" accepted alias). sort Logical. Sort loadings size within component? Default TRUE. blank Numeric. Suppress (hide) loadings absolute value threshold print output. Default 0.40 (matches SPSS BLANK(.40)). Set 0 show loadings. na.rm Logical. Remove missing values? Default TRUE.

title: Explore the Structure Behind Your Survey Items — efa
text: efa result object containing: loadings Component loading matrix (rotated rotation applied) unrotated_loadings Unrotated component matrix eigenvalues eigenvalues correlation matrix variance_explained Tibble initial eigenvalues: Total, % Variance, Cumulative % (one row per variable) extraction_variance Tibble extraction sums squared loadings extracted components/factors (SPSS "Extraction Sums Squared Loadings"). ML variance common factors explain - figure compact print reports. rotation_variance Tibble rotation sums squared loadings (oblique rotations column sums squares structure matrix, SPSS reports ) communalities Extraction communalities variable kmo List overall KMO per-item MSA values bartlett List chi_sq, df, p_value rotation Rotation method used extraction Extraction method used n_factors Number components extracted correlation_matrix Correlation matrix used analysis initial_communalities Initial communalities (1.0 PCA, SMC ML) goodness_of_fit Goodness--fit test (ML ): chi_sq, df, p_value. NULL PCA. uniquenesses Unique variances per variable (ML , NULL PCA) pattern_matrix Pattern matrix (oblimin/promax , NULL otherwise) structure_matrix Structure matrix (oblimin/promax , NULL otherwise) factor_correlations Factor correlation matrix (oblimin/promax , NULL otherwise) rotation_iterations, rotation_converged Iterations rotation SPSS counts ("Rotation converged 4 iterations"; promax varimax step) whether converged; NULL without rotation variables Character vector variable names variable_labels Named character vector variable labels (NA variable none); summary() shows next names, shortened console width tables weights Weights variable name NULL item_statistics Tibble mean, SD, analysis N missing N per item. use = "pairwise" item uses valid cases; use = "complete" items use complete cases. n Sample size: smallest pairwise N (use = "pairwise", N Bartlett's test SPSS) number complete cases (use = "complete"); sum weights weighted use missing-data handling used ("pairwise" "complete") col_prefix Column name prefix: "PC" PCA, "Factor" ML sort Whether loadings sorted blank Suppression threshold Use summary() full SPSS-style output toggleable sections.

title: Explore the Structure Behind Your Survey Items — efa
text: KMO (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin) measures sampling adequacy: KMO > 0.90: Marvelous KMO 0.80 - 0.90: Meritorious KMO 0.70 - 0.80: Middling KMO 0.60 - 0.70: Mediocre KMO 0.50 - 0.60: Miserable KMO < 0.50: Unacceptable - use factor analysis Bartlett's Test Sphericity tests whether correlations significantly different zero. significant result (p < .05) means correlation matrix suitable factor analysis. Eigenvalues indicate much variance component explains. Kaiser criterion retains components eigenvalue > 1. Factor Loadings show strongly item relates component: |loading| > 0.70: Strong association |loading| 0.40 - 0.70: Moderate association |loading| < 0.40: Weak (suppressed default) Communalities show much item's variance explained extracted components. Low communalities (< 0.40) suggest item fit well others.

title: Explore the Structure Behind Your Survey Items — efa
text: PCA (default): Extracts components explaining maximum total variance. Simple robust. assume normality. ML: Extracts factors explaining shared variance . Assumes multivariate normality. Provides goodness--fit test evaluate model fit. non-significant chi-square (p > .05) suggests adequate fit.

title: Explore the Structure Behind Your Survey Items — efa
text: Varimax (default): Assumes factors uncorrelated. Produces simpler, easier--interpret results. Oblimin: Allows factors correlated. realistic social science data. Produces Pattern Matrix (unique contributions) Structure Matrix (total correlations). Promax: Oblique rotation based power transformation Varimax results. Like Oblimin, produces Pattern Structure matrices. Common alternative Oblimin SPSS. None: rotation. Rarely useful interpretation.

what: Compare Groups Across Multiple Factors: Factorial ANOVA — factorial_anova
title: Compare Groups Across Multiple Factors: Factorial ANOVA — factorial_anova
text: factorial_anova() tests whether group means differ across two factors simultaneously, including interactions. performs factorial (two-way, three-way) ANOVA using Type III Sum Squares, matching SPSS UNIANOVA output. Think : Testing multiple grouping variables Detecting interaction effects (factor combinations matter?) extension one-way ANOVA multiple factors test tells : Whether factor main effect outcome Whether factors interact (effect one depends ) much variance factor explains (partial eta squared)

title: Compare Groups Across Multiple Factors: Factorial ANOVA — factorial_anova
code: factorial_anova(data, dv, between, weights = NULL, ss_type = 3)

title: Compare Groups Across Multiple Factors: Factorial ANOVA — factorial_anova
text: data survey data (data frame tibble) dv numeric dependent variable analyze (unquoted) Character vector unquoted variable names specifying -subjects factors (2-3 factors). must categorical variables (factor, character, labelled numeric). weights Optional survey weights population-representative results. Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. ss_type Deprecated; 3 (Type III, SPSS default) implemented. Passing 2 issues warning computes Type III.

Significant main effect = group means differ factor Example: Education affects income regardless gender Interaction Effects: effect one factor depend another? Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. use handle missing data: "listwise" (default) drops case missing value variable (matching SPSS /MISSING LISTWISE). "pairwise" computes regression pairwise covariance/correlation matrix, retaining cases (matching SPSS /MISSING PAIRWISE). standardized Logical. TRUE (default), standardized coefficients (Beta) calculated included output. conf.level Confidence level coefficient intervals (default 0.95). factors factor predictors entered model: "dummy" (default, matches base R lm()) expands factor L levels L - 1 contrasts; "numeric" silently coerces factor levels integer codes, matching SPSS REGRESSION default behavior (ordinal--scale). Used predictors formula given. Must exactly two distinct values (e.g. 0/1, 1/2, two-level factor); see Technical Details. predictors Predictor variable(s) (unquoted, supports tidyselect). Used dependent formula given. dependent, weights grouping variables never used predictors (selection (.numeric) drops message). Character predictors entered factors. weights Optional survey weights. specified, weighted maximum likelihood estimation used, matching SPSS WEIGHT behavior. Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. conf.level Confidence level odds ratio intervals (default 0.95). factors factor predictors entered model: "dummy" (default, matches base R glm()) expands factor L levels L - 1 contrasts; "numeric" silently coerces factor levels integer codes, matching SPSS LOGISTIC REGRESSION default behavior /CATEGORICAL subcommand given. "numeric" mode emits one-line cli::cli_inform() listing coerced variables. Note ordered factors, "dummy" applies R's default polynomial contrasts (terms suffixed .L, .Q, .C), treatment dummies; convert factor(x, ordered = FALSE) first want dummy coding. factors applies factors : labelled predictors SPSS files (haven_labelled) numeric enter numeric codes, SPSS LOGISTIC REGRESSION without /CATEGORICAL; summary() notes . EXP(B)" summary), profile-likelihood intervals via confint(model, method = "profile"); see confint.logistic_regression. grouped data, returns list class "logistic_regression" $groups holding one fitted glm-inheriting result per group.

title: Run a Logistic Regression — logistic_regression
text: output includes five sections matching SPSS LOGISTIC REGRESSION output: Omnibus Test: Tests whether model whole significant. significant chi-square means model predicts better chance. Model Summary: -2 Log Likelihood pseudo R-squared values. Lower -2LL = better fit. Higher R-squared = variance explained. Hosmer-Lemeshow Test: Goodness--fit test. non-significant result (p > 0.05) means model fits data well. Classification Table: well model classifies cases. Shows percentage correctly predicted group overall. Coefficients: B, Wald test, odds ratios (Exp(B)), CIs. Interpreting odds ratios (Exp(B)): Exp(B) > 1: Predictor increases odds outcome Exp(B) < 1: Predictor decreases odds outcome Exp(B) = 1: Predictor effect odds

title: Run a Logistic Regression — logistic_regression
text: Use logistic_regression() : dependent variable binary (yes/, 0/1, pass/fail) want predict group membership one predictors need odds ratios interpret predictor effects continuous outcomes, use linear_regression instead.

title: Run a Logistic Regression — logistic_regression
text: Dependent Variable: variable exactly two distinct observed values, coded internally 0/1 like SPSS LOGISTIC REGRESSION : numeric labelled variables lower value becomes 0 higher 1 (1/2 0/1 codings give model); factors unused levels dropped first remaining level becomes 0; character values ordered alphabetically; logicals code FALSE = 0, TRUE = 1. model predicts probability category coded 1 - compact print names ([P(y = category)]), summary() shows SPSS "Dependent Variable Encoding" table (also stored $dv_encoding). grouped analysis uses one encoding groups. Missing Data: Listwise deletion used (matching SPSS LOGISTIC REGRESSION default behavior). Weights: weights specified, treated frequency weights (matching SPSS WEIGHT behavior). Pseudo R-squared: Three measures reported: Cox & Snell R-squared (bounded 1) Nagelkerke R-squared (adjusted reach 1) McFadden R-squared (1 - LL_model/LL_null) Factor Predictors: default (factors = "dummy"), factor predictors expanded L - 1 contrasts via R's stats::model.matrix(), matching base R glm(): unordered factors get treatment (dummy) contrasts first level, ordered factors get R's default polynomial contrasts (.L/.Q/.C terms). Pass factors = "numeric" silently coerce factor levels integer codes (SPSS LOGISTIC REGRESSION default without explicit /CATEGORICAL subcommand). Grouped Analysis: data grouped via dplyr::group_by(), separate regression run group (matching SPSS SPLIT FILE ).

title: Compare Two Groups Without Assuming Normal Data — mann_whitney
text: data survey data (data frame tibble) ... variables want compare groups. can list multiple variables use helpers like starts_with("satisfaction") group categorical variable defines two groups (e.g., gender, treatment/control). Must exactly two groups. weights Optional survey weights population-representative results. Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. mu hypothesized location shift group 1 group 2 (Default: 0, meaning difference; SPSS test). wilcox.test(), group-1 values shifted mu ranking, U, W, Z, r p refer hypothesis. mu = 0 available weights. alternative Direction test: "two.sided" (default): Test groups different. Z reported SPSS , smaller U (never positive). "greater": Test group 1 > group 2 "less": Test group 1 < group 2 one-sided test Z directional (positive group 1 tends higher values), sign matches p-value. conf.level used. Rank tests report confidence interval (SPSS NPAR TESTS neither); kept backward compatibility.

title: Compare Two Groups Without Assuming Normal Data — mann_whitney
text: Test results showing whether groups differ, including: U W statistics (test statistics) Z-score p-value (groups different?) Effect size r (r_effect, big difference?) Rank means group (group higher?) Use summary() full SPSS-style output toggleable sections.

title: Compare Two Groups Without Assuming Normal Data — mann_whitney
text: P-value: p < 0.05, groups significantly different p < 0.001: strong evidence difference p < 0.01: Strong evidence difference p < 0.05: Moderate evidence difference p >= 0.05: significant difference found Effect Size r (big difference?): |r| < 0.1: Negligible difference 0.1 < 0.3: Small difference 0.3 < 0.5: Medium difference 0.5 higher: Large difference Rank Mean Difference: Positive: Group 1 tends higher values Negative: Group 2 tends higher values Zero: Groups similar distributions

what: Transform Scores to Percent of Maximum Possible (POMPS) — pomps
title: Transform Scores to Percent of Maximum Possible (POMPS) — pomps
text: pomps() transforms scores 0-100 scale using Percent Maximum Possible Scores method. makes different scales directly comparable regardless original range. R equivalent SPSS formula: COMPUTE v81p = ((v81 - 1) / (7 - 1)) * 100. score 0 means minimum possible score, 100 means maximum. transformation preserves correlations variables.

title: Transform Scores to Percent of Maximum Possible (POMPS) — pomps
code: pomps(x, scale_min = NULL, scale_max = NULL)

title: Transform Scores to Percent of Maximum Possible (POMPS) — pomps
text: x numeric vector transform (e.g., column data). scale_min theoretical minimum scale. NULL (default), observed minimum x used. scale_max theoretical maximum scale. NULL (default), observed maximum x used.

title: Transform Scores to Percent of Maximum Possible (POMPS) — pomps
text: numeric vector length x, values rescaled 0-100 range. variable label x kept; missing values (including SPSS missing types imported data) become plain NA, SPSS COMPUTE.

title: Transform Scores to Percent of Maximum Possible (POMPS) — pomps
text: POMPS = ((score - scale_min) / (scale_max - scale_min)) * 100

title: Transform Scores to Percent of Maximum Possible (POMPS) — pomps
text: default, pomps() uses observed minimum maximum data. However, Likert scales specify theoretical range: 1-5 Likert scale: scale_min = 1, scale_max = 5 1-7 Likert scale: scale_min = 1, scale_max = 7 0-10 scale: scale_min = 0, scale_max = 10 Using theoretical values ensures transformation consistent across samples time points. Values outside range (e.g. unrecoded "know" = 9 1-5 scale) give scores 0 100; pomps() warns , recode missing codes first.

title: Transform Scores to Percent of Maximum Possible (POMPS) — pomps
text: Comparing variables measured different scales Creating profile plots across scales different ranges Reporting scale scores intuitive 0-100 format

title: Transform Scores to Percent of Maximum Possible (POMPS) — pomps
code: library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Transform a 1-5 Likert scale to POMPS survey_data <- survey_data %>%   mutate(trust_gov_pomps = pomps(trust_government, scale_min = 1, scale_max = 5))  # Transform multiple variables with the same scale survey_data <- survey_data %>%   mutate(across(     c(trust_government, trust_media, trust_science),     ~ pomps(.x, scale_min = 1, scale_max = 5),     .names = "{.col}_pomps"   ))  # Auto-detect range (uses observed min/max) survey_data <- survey_data %>%   mutate(age_pomps = pomps(age))

text: single values ranges accept decimals (e.g. "3.6=2" "2.5:3.5=1"). Single-value matching compares values strings (rounded 15 significant digits), decimal codes match reliably even stored floating-point representation error.

title: Recode Variables Using String Syntax — rec
text: can attach value labels directly rules string using square brackets new value: "1:2=1 [Low]; 3=2 [Medium]; 4:5=3 [High]" equivalent specifying val_labels = c("1" = "Low", "2" = "Medium", "3" = "High") compact self-documenting. inline labels val_labels provided, val_labels takes precedence.

title: Recode Variables Using String Syntax — rec
text: "rev" reverses scale computing hi + lo - x. scale range lo-hi taken value labels valid codes (together observed values), item answered 2-5 labelled 1-5 scale becomes 4-1, 5-2. Without value labels observed minimum maximum used message says ; set range explicitly "rev(lo, hi)", e.g. rules = "rev(1, 5)". Value labels mirrored accordingly; missing values keep type. "dicho" dichotomizes median: values \(\le\) median become 0, values \(>\) median become 1. "dicho(x)" dichotomizes fixed cut-point x: values \(\le x\) become 0, values \(> x\) become 1. "mean" dichotomizes arithmetic mean: values \(\le\) mean become 0, values \(>\) mean become 1. "quart" splits four quartile groups using quantile(): values \(\le\) Q1 become 1, Q1–Q2 become 2, Q2–Q3 become 3, \(>\) Q3 become 4. Quartile boundaries computed unweighted.

title: Recode Variables Using String Syntax — rec
code: library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Collapse a 5-point scale to 3 categories (inline labels) data <- rec(survey_data, trust_government,             rules = "1:2=1 [Low]; 3=2 [Medium]; 4:5=3 [High]")  # Reverse a scale (with suffix to keep original) data <- rec(survey_data, trust_government, trust_media,             rules = "rev(1, 5)", suffix = "_r")  # Dichotomize at the median data <- rec(survey_data, age, rules = "dicho", suffix = "_d")  # Set missing value codes to NA data <- rec(survey_data, starts_with("trust"),             rules = "-9=NA; -8=NA; else=copy")  # Replace NA with 0 data <- rec(survey_data, trust_government,             rules = "NA=0; else=copy")  # Quartile split data <- rec(survey_data, age, rules = "quart", suffix = "_q")  # Use inside mutate() survey_data <- survey_data %>%   mutate(     trust_gov_3 = rec(trust_government,                       rules = "1:2=1 [Low]; 3=2 [Medium]; 4:5=3 [High]"),     age_q = rec(age, rules = "quart")   )

text: reliability() calculates Cronbach's Alpha, McDonald's Omega, detailed item statistics evaluate whether survey items form reliable scale. R equivalent SPSS's RELIABILITY /MODEL=ALPHA /STATISTICS=DESCRIPTIVE CORR /SUMMARY=TOTAL. example, 3 items measuring "trust", reliability analysis tells whether items consistently measure concept.

text: data survey data (data frame tibble) ... items analyze. Use bare column names separated commas, tidyselect helpers like starts_with("trust"). weights Optional survey weights population-representative results. Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. na.rm Remove missing values calculating? (Default: TRUE). Uses listwise deletion (complete cases across items).

title: Check How Reliably Your Scale Measures a Concept — reliability
text: reliability result object containing: alpha Cronbach's Alpha (unstandardized) alpha_standardized Cronbach's Alpha based standardized items omega McDonald's Omega (raw/total, one-factor ML model; NA fewer 3 items) omega_std Standardized Omega (correlation metric) n_items Number items scale item_statistics Mean, SD, N item item_total Corrected Item-Total Correlation, Alpha Item Deleted, Omega Item Deleted inter_item_cor Inter-item correlation matrix n Sample size (listwise) variable_labels Named character vector items' variable labels (NA item none); summary() lists next item names removed_items Items removed zero variance, NULL negative_items alpha negative: items negative corrected item-total correlation (candidates reverse-coding) Use summary() full SPSS-style output toggleable sections.

title: Check How Reliably Your Scale Measures a Concept — reliability
text: Cronbach's Alpha tells internally consistent scale : Alpha > 0.90: Excellent reliability Alpha 0.80 - 0.90: Good reliability Alpha 0.70 - 0.80: Acceptable reliability Alpha 0.60 - 0.70: Questionable reliability Alpha < 0.60: Poor reliability - reconsider items Item-Total Correlation shows well item fits scale: Values > 0.40: Item fits well Values 0.20 - 0.40: Item may need review Values < 0.20: Consider removing item Alpha Item Deleted shows happens remove item: alpha increases removing item, item hurts reliability alpha decreases, item contributes scale

title: Check How Reliably Your Scale Measures a Concept — reliability
text: McDonald's Omega (omega total) factor-model-based reliability coefficient. alpha assumes every item measures construct equally well (tau-equivalence), omega fits one-factor model lets item carry loading. two agree items roughly tau-equivalent; omega typically slightly higher (accurate estimate) loadings differ across items, common case survey scales (Hayes & Coutts, 2020). reliability() reports two variants, mirroring two alpha variants: omega covariance metric (analogous raw alpha) omega_std correlation metric (analogous standardized alpha). Omega Item Deleted refits one-factor model without item, mirroring Alpha Item Deleted. one-factor model needs least 3 items identified: fewer 3 items omega fields NA (alpha still computed), Omega Item Deleted NA whenever reduced scale fall 3 items. Omega also NA, warning, items' correlation matrix singular one-factor solution Heywood case (item's uniqueness lower bound, .e. loading 1: "factor" single item, scale). Items zero variance removed scale warning, SPSS RELIABILITY ($removed_items).

title: Check How Reliably Your Scale Measures a Concept — reliability
text: Cronbach's alpha item statistics reproduce SPSS v29 RELIABILITY output, weighted unweighted.
