code: # Load required packages and data library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Perform ANOVA followed by Scheffe post-hoc test anova_result <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education)  # Scheffe post-hoc comparisons anova_result %>% scheffe_test() #> Scheffe Post-Hoc Test by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 4 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Multiple variables anova_result_multi <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, income, group = education)  anova_result_multi %>% scheffe_test() #> Scheffe Post-Hoc Test by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 4 significant (p < .05) #>   income: 6 comparisons, 6 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Weighted analysis anova_weighted <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education, weights = sampling_weight)  anova_weighted %>% scheffe_test() #> Scheffe Post-Hoc Test by education [Weighted] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 4 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Grouped analysis anova_grouped <- survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education)  anova_grouped %>% scheffe_test() #> Scheffe Post-Hoc Test by education #> [region = East] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 2 significant (p < .05) #> [region = West] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 4 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Custom confidence level (99%) anova_result %>% scheffe_test(conf.level = 0.99) #> Scheffe Post-Hoc Test by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 4 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.

code: std(data, ..., method = "sd", weights = NULL, suffix = NULL, na.rm = TRUE)

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: data data frame numeric vector. ... Variables standardize (tidyselect). used data data frame. method Standardization method: "sd" Standard z-score: (x - mean) / sd (default) "2sd" Gelman's 2-SD method: (x - mean) / (2 * sd). Useful regression binary predictors. "mad" Robust: (x - median) / mad. Resistant outliers. "gmd" Gini's Mean Difference: (x - mean) / gmd. robust alternative. weights Optional survey weights. provided, weighted mean weighted SD used standardization. supported methods "sd" "2sd". Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. suffix character string appended column names (e.g., "_z"). NULL (default), original columns overwritten. na.rm Remove missing values computing mean SD? Default: TRUE.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: data vector, standardized numeric vector. data data frame, modified data frame (invisibly).

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: sd (default): Standard z-transformation. Mean = 0, SD = 1. 2sd: Divides 2 standard deviations (Gelman, 2008). makes standardized continuous predictors comparable binary predictors regression. mad: Uses Median Absolute Deviation instead SD. Robust outliers. gmd: Uses Gini's Mean Difference — robust spread measure based pairwise absolute differences.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: weights provided, weighted mean weighted standard deviation (using SPSS frequency weight formula) used. supported methods "sd" "2sd". robust methods "mad" "gmd" support weights.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: data grouped (via group_by()), standardization performed separately within group. useful within-group comparisons. Weights also subsetted per group.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
text: result plain numeric variable (value labels dropped, variable label kept " (standardized)" appended). Missing values imported data, including SPSS missing types, become plain NA – SPSS's DESCRIPTIVES /SAVE gives system-missing z-scores.

title: Standardize Variables (Z-Scores) — std
code: library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Standard z-scores data <- std(survey_data, age, income, suffix = "_z")  # Gelman 2-SD standardization (for regression) data <- std(survey_data, income, age, method = "2sd",             suffix = "_z")  # Robust standardization data <- std(survey_data, income, method = "mad", suffix = "_z")  # Weighted standardization data <- std(survey_data, income, age,             weights = sampling_weight, suffix = "_z")  # Group-wise standardization data <- survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   std(income, suffix = "_z")

what: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: t_test() helps determine two groups different average values. example, men women different satisfaction scores? Region spend Region B? year better last year? test tells : Whether difference statistically significant big difference (effect sizes) likely range true difference (confidence interval)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
code: t_test(   data,   ...,   group = NULL,   weights = NULL,   var.equal = FALSE,   mu = 0,   alternative = c("two.sided", "less", "greater"),   conf.level = 0.95 )

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: data survey data (data frame tibble) ... numeric variables test. List multiple variables use tidyselect helpers like starts_with("trust"). group variable defines two groups (e.g., gender, region). Must exactly two categories. Leave empty one-sample tests. weights Optional survey weights population-representative results. Give column name (unquoted string), expression sampling_weight * 2, numeric vector one weight per row. var.equal assume equal variances? (Default: FALSE) FALSE: Safer, works even groups vary differently (Welch's test) TRUE: Traditional approach, assumes equal spread (Student's test) mu Comparison value (Default: 0). two-sample tests, usually 0. one-sample tests, benchmark value. alternative Direction test: "two.sided" (default): difference "greater": First group higher "less": First group lower conf.level Confidence level intervals (Default: 0.95 = 95%)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: Test results showing whether groups differ, including: t-statistic p-value statistical significance Mean difference confidence interval (one-sample tests: mean minus mu interval difference, SPSS One-Sample Test) Effect sizes (Cohen's d, Hedges' g, Glass' Delta) Group statistics (mean, SD, standard error mean, sample size) note column explains variable (group) computed, e.g. variance one group valid data Use summary() full SPSS-style output toggleable sections.

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: P-value: difference statistically significant? p < 0.001: strong evidence difference p < 0.01: Strong evidence difference p < 0.05: Moderate evidence difference p >= 0.05: significant difference found Effect Sizes (big difference?): Cohen's d: standard measure |d| < 0.2: Negligible difference |d| = 0.2-0.5: Small difference |d| = 0.5-0.8: Medium difference |d| > 0.8: Large difference Hedges' g: Corrected small samples Glass' Delta: Uses control group SD Confidence Interval: Range true difference likely falls includes 0, groups may differ Width indicates precision (narrower = precise)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: Use t-test : exactly two groups compare outcome variable numeric (continuous) Groups independent (different people ) Data roughly normally distributed (n >= 30 per group) use : two groups (use ANOVA) Data severely skewed small samples (use Mann-Whitney) Groups paired matched (use wilcoxon_test()) Variables categorical (use chi-square)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: results show variance assumptions: Welch's test (var.equal = FALSE): Safer, assume equal variances Student's test (var.equal = TRUE): Traditional, assumes equal variances result t = 2.45, p = 0.015, d = 0.62 means: Groups 2.45 standard errors apart (t-statistic) 1.5% chance due random variation (p-value) Medium-sized practical difference (Cohen's d)

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: Always check sample sizes (aim 30+ per group) Consider statistical significance effect size Use weights population-level conclusions Plot data first check assumptions Report confidence intervals along p-values

title: Test If Two Groups Differ — t_test
text: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates. Hedges, L. V. (1981). Distribution theory Glass's estimator effect size related estimators. Journal Educational Statistics, 6(2), 107-128. Glass, G. V. (1976). Primary, secondary, meta-analysis research. Educational Researcher, 5(10), 3-8. Welch, B. L. (1947). generalization "Student's" problem several different population variances involved. Biometrika, 34(1-2), 28-35.

code: # Load required packages and data library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Basic two-sample test survey_data %>%   t_test(life_satisfaction, group = gender) #> t-Test: life_satisfaction by gender #>   t(2384.1) = -1.018, p = 0.309, g = -0.041 (negligible), N = 2421 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # With survey weights survey_data %>%   t_test(life_satisfaction, group = gender, weights = sampling_weight) #> t-Test: life_satisfaction by gender [Weighted] #>   t(2391.3) = -1.069, p = 0.285, g = -0.043 (negligible), N = 2436 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # Multiple variables survey_data %>%   t_test(age, income, life_satisfaction, group = region, weights = sampling_weight) #> t-Test: age by region [Weighted] #>   t(763.8) = 2.551, p = 0.011 *, g = 0.130 (negligible), N = 2516 #> t-Test: income by region [Weighted] #>   t(713.7) = 0.299, p = 0.765, g = 0.016 (negligible), N = 2200 #> t-Test: life_satisfaction by region [Weighted] #>   t(721.0) = -0.031, p = 0.975, g = -0.002 (negligible), N = 2437 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # One-sample test against a benchmark survey_data %>%   t_test(life_satisfaction, mu = 5, weights = sampling_weight) #> t-Test: life_satisfaction [Weighted] #>   t(2435.6) = -58.916, p < 0.001 ***, N = 2437 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # Grouped analysis survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   t_test(life_satisfaction, group = gender, weights = sampling_weight) #> [region = East] #> t-Test: life_satisfaction by gender [Weighted] #>   t(484.7) = 0.641, p = 0.522, g = 0.058 (negligible), N = 488 #> [region = West] #> t-Test: life_satisfaction by gender [Weighted] #>   t(1901.1) = -1.548, p = 0.122, g = -0.070 (negligible), N = 1949 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # Equal variance assumption survey_data %>%   t_test(life_satisfaction, group = gender, var.equal = TRUE) #> t-Test: life_satisfaction by gender #>   t(2419) = -1.019, p = 0.308, g = -0.041 (negligible), N = 2421 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # Using tidyselect helpers survey_data %>%   t_test(starts_with("trust"), group = gender, weights = sampling_weight) #> t-Test: trust_government by gender [Weighted] #>   t(2322.8) = -0.682, p = 0.496, g = -0.028 (negligible), N = 2371 #> t-Test: trust_media by gender [Weighted] #>   t(2350.1) = -2.196, p = 0.028 *, g = -0.090 (negligible), N = 2382 #> t-Test: trust_science by gender [Weighted] #>   t(2360.9) = -1.421, p = 0.156, g = -0.058 (negligible), N = 2414 #> Use summary() for detailed output.  # title: Convert Labelled Variables to Character — to_character

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Character — to_character

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Character — to_character
text: data data frame, tibble, single vector. ... Optional: unquoted variable names (tidyselect supported). empty, converts every haven_labelled column whose values value-labelled (metric variables left unchanged message, to_label()). drop_na TRUE (default), tagged NAs become regular NA. add_non_labelled TRUE, unlabelled values included numeric string representation. Default: FALSE. drop.na, add.non.labelled Defunct dot-case argument names, removed mariposa 0.6.9. Calling function error; use snake_case equivalents instead. (formals retained old names error clearly instead swallowed ....)

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Character — to_character
text: input labelled variables converted character. single vector input, returns character vector.

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Character — to_character
text: convenience wrapper around to_label() calls .character() result. Use need character output (e.g., string operations) rather factor output. variable label ("label" attribute) preserved output.

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: Creates 0/1 dummy variables categorical variables. Column names derived value labels available, making results readable SPSS-style data. Unlike model.matrix(), to_dummy() uses value labels column naming handles haven_labelled vectors correctly.

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
code: to_dummy(data, ..., suffix = "val", ref = NULL, append = TRUE)

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: data data frame vector. data frame passed, use ... select variables. ... Variables dummy-code (tidyselect). used data data frame. suffix name dummy columns: "val" (default) uses raw value (e.g., gender_1), "label" uses value label (e.g., gender_Male). ref value use reference category (omitted output). NULL (default), categories get dummy variable. Set specific value n-1 coding (e.g., regression). factor, give level name (ref = "Male") number: original code to_label() factor, otherwise level position (ref = 1 = first level). ref matches category error. append TRUE (default), dummy columns appended original data frame. FALSE, dummy columns returned. Ignored data vector.

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: append = TRUE (default), original data frame dummy columns appended. append = FALSE, tibble dummy columns. vector input, always tibble dummy columns.

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: suffix = "val": {varname}_{value} (e.g., gender_1, gender_2). suffix = "label": {varname}_{label} labels cleaned (umlauts transliterated, e.g. "männlich" -> maennlich; spaces replaced _; special characters removed). Values without usable label (e.g. "..") use value; labels shared several values get value appended, every category keeps column.

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
text: regression, typically need n-1 dummy variables. Set ref value reference category omit .

title: Create Dummy Variables (One-Hot Encoding) — to_dummy
code: library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Create dummies and append to data (default) data <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender)  # Use labels for column names data <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender, suffix = "label")  # n-1 dummies with reference category data <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender, ref = 1)  # Multiple variables data <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender, education, suffix = "label")  # Return only the dummy columns (without original data) dummies <- to_dummy(survey_data, gender, append = FALSE)

what: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
text: Converts haven_labelled variables factors, using value labels factor levels. primary function making labelled survey data ready plotting, cross-tabulation, regression analysis.

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
code: to_label(   data,   ...,   ordered = FALSE,   drop_na = TRUE,   drop_unused = FALSE,   add_non_labelled = FALSE,   drop.na = NULL,   drop.unused = NULL,   add.non.labelled = NULL )

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
text: data data frame, tibble, single vector. ... Optional: unquoted variable names (tidyselect supported). empty, converts every haven_labelled column whose values value-labelled; metric variables (e.g. age labels missing codes), weights partially labelled variables left unchanged message. Selected variables always converted. ordered TRUE, creates ordered factor. Default: FALSE. drop_na TRUE (default), tagged NAs converted regular NA (excluded factor levels). FALSE, tagged NAs kept factor levels label text. drop_unused TRUE, removes factor levels zero observations. Default: FALSE. add_non_labelled TRUE, values without labels included factor levels using numeric value level name. Default: FALSE (unlabelled values become NA, warning naming variables). drop.na, drop.unused, add.non.labelled Defunct dot-case argument names, removed mariposa 0.6.9. Calling function error; use snake_case equivalents instead. (formals retained old names error clearly instead swallowed ....)

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
text: input labelled variables converted factors. single vector input, returns factor.

title: Convert Labelled Variables to Factors — to_label
text: labelled variable, numeric codes replaced associated value labels. resulting factor levels ordered original numeric values (alphabetically). Distinct codes share label text (e.g. ".." unlabelled points scale) stay distinct levels code appended: ".. (2)", ".. (3)". original code every level kept factor's "codes" attribute (named numeric vector, names = levels), to_numeric() to_labelled() can restore original values (e.g. 6, 42, 90) instead renumbering levels 1, 2, 3. attribute survives dplyr verbs (filter(), mutate(), arrange(), ...) , like variable label, dropped base subsetting (x[]) longer applies levels renamed extended.

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
text: tukey_test() tells exactly groups different ANOVA finds overall differences. like follow-investigation pinpoints differences lie. Think : ANOVA says "differences somewhere" Tukey test says "specifically, Group differs Group C" way make possible comparisons controlling error rates

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
text: x ANOVA results oneway_anova() conf.level Confidence level simultaneous intervals (Default: 0.95). SPSS corresponds post-hoc ALPHA (1 - alpha) follow conf.level oneway_anova(), (like SPSS CILEVEL) sets intervals group means. ... Additional arguments (currently unused)

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
text: Pairwise comparison results showing: group pairs significantly different Size difference pair Adjusted p-values (controlling multiple comparisons) Confidence intervals difference

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
text: Adjusted P-values: Control multiple comparisons p < 0.05: Groups significantly different p >= 0.05: significant difference groups make many comparisons, chance alone produce false positives Tukey adjustment protects conservative Mean Differences: Positive: First group higher average second Negative: Second group higher average first Zero confidence interval: significant difference

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
text: Use Tukey test : ANOVA shows significant differences (p < 0.05) want know specific groups differ need compare possible pairs Group sizes roughly equal Variances roughly equal across groups

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
text: Tukey Test: Less conservative (easier find differences) Best equal group sizes Protects pairwise comparisons Narrower confidence intervals Scheffe Test: conservative (hardest find differences) Best unequal group sizes Protects possible comparisons Wider confidence intervals

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
text: Example: "Group - Group B: Diff = 3.2, p = 0.012" Group 's average 3.2 units higher Group B's difference statistically significant (p < 0.05) can confident groups truly differ

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
text: run post-hoc tests ANOVA significant Focus comparisons make theoretical sense Consider practical significance, just statistical Report difference confidence interval Remember: non-significant mean "exactly equal"

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
text: Tukey, J. W. (1949). Comparing individual means analysis variance. Biometrics, 5(2), 99-114. Kramer, C. Y. (1956). Extension multiple range tests group means unequal numbers replications. Biometrics, 12(3), 307-310.

title: Find Which Specific Groups Differ After ANOVA — tukey_test
code: # Load required packages and data library(dplyr) data(survey_data)  # Perform ANOVA followed by Tukey post-hoc test anova_result <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education)  # Tukey post-hoc comparisons anova_result %>% tukey_test() #> Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test by education #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # With weights anova_weighted <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education, weights = sampling_weight)  anova_weighted %>% tukey_test() #> Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test by education [Weighted] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Multiple variables anova_multi <- survey_data %>%   oneway_anova(trust_government, trust_science, group = education)  anova_multi %>% tukey_test() #> Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test by education #>   trust_government: 6 comparisons, 0 significant (p < .05) #>   trust_science: 6 comparisons, 0 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.  # Grouped analysis anova_grouped <- survey_data %>%   group_by(region) %>%   oneway_anova(life_satisfaction, group = education)  anova_grouped %>% tukey_test() #> Tukey HSD Post-Hoc Test by education #> [region = East] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 2 significant (p < .05) #> [region = West] #>   life_satisfaction: 6 comparisons, 5 significant (p < .05) #> Use summary() for the full comparison table.

title: Measure Population-Representative Kurtosis — w_kurtosis
text: Uses SPSS Type 2 (sample-corrected) excess kurtosis formula. First, population excess kurtosis (\(g_2\)) calculated: \(g_2 = \frac{m_4}{m_2^2} - 3\) \(m_2 = \sum w_i(x_i - \bar{x}_w)^2 / V_1\) \(m_4 = \sum w_i(x_i - \bar{x}_w)^4 / V_1\) \(V_1 = \sum w_i\). , bias-corrected (Type 2) kurtosis : \(G_2 = \frac{(n+1) \cdot g_2 + 6}{(n-2)(n-3)} \cdot (n-1)\) \(n = V_1\) weighted data.

text: New fisher_test() performs Fisher’s exact test independence, recommended small samples expected cell counts 5; supports weights, multiple variables group_by(). New chisq_gof() tests whether categorical variable follows expected distribution (equal proportions default, custom proportions), residuals, weights multiple variables. New mcnemar_test() tests changes paired proportions two dichotomous measurements (e.g. /), asymptotic exact p-values, 2x2 table, continuity correction weights. New dunn_test() performs Dunn’s pairwise post-hoc comparisons kruskal_wallis() results, adjustable p-value correction (Bonferroni, Holm, BH others). title: mariposa 0.3.0
text: New kruskal_wallis() compares three independent groups ordinal data (non-parametric alternative one-way ANOVA), effect size, weights, group_by() multiple variables. New wilcoxon_test() compares two paired measurements (Wilcoxon signed-rank test), rank categories (negative, positive, ties) effect size r. New friedman_test() compares three related measurements (non-parametric alternative repeated-measures ANOVA), Kendall’s W effect size. New binomial_test() tests whether observed proportion matches expected value (exact binomial test), one binary variables.

text: New reliability() computes Cronbach’s alpha item statistics: corrected item-total correlations, alpha item deleted, inter-item correlation matrix. New scale_index() computes mean indices across items, min_valid like SPSS MEAN.x(). New pomps() rescales values percent maximum possible scores (0-100). New linear_regression() fits linear models SPSS-style output (coefficients B, SE, Beta, t p; ANOVA table; R, R-squared adjusted R-squared), using formula SPSS-style dependent/predictors interface.
